slides.text: At two in the afternoon I noticed three Instagram posts hadn't gone up — 6am, 9am, noon, all missed.

citations.quote: At two in the afternoon I noticed three Instagram posts hadn't gone up — 6am, 9am, noon, all missed.

slides.text: The job had been crashing on every single run, without exception, since the day I'd first set it up. Same error every time: macOS quietly refusing it read access to a folder on my Desktop, forty-four times over.

citations.quote: The job had been crashing on every single run, without exception, since the day I'd first set it up.
Same error every time: macOS quietly refusing it read access to a folder on my Desktop, forty-four times over.

slides.text: Here's the part that actually mattered: when I ran the exact same script by hand, from my own terminal, it worked. My shell already had the permission — granted once, years ago, without me thinking about it.

citations.quote: Here's the part that actually mattered: when I ran the exact same script by hand, from my own terminal, it worked.

slides.text: I'd tested the script. I hadn't tested the absence of me.

citations.quote: I hadn't tested the absence of me.

slides.text: Kieran Klaassen — who runs 44 AI agents across Every's projects, not three Instagram slots — has a name for the order I'd quietly jumped: build it, use it, trust it, and then orchestrate it.

citations.quote: Kieran Klaassen — who runs 44 AI agents across Every's projects, not three Instagram slots — has a name for the order I'd quietly jumped: build it, use it, trust it, and then orchestrate it.

slides.text: agents sitting frozen on "working" with no signal anything's wrong One job or forty-four, the failure that survives every manual test is the one you only meet in the room you stopped standing in.

citations.quote: agents sitting frozen on "working" with no signal anything's wrong

slides.text: Jake Van Clief works on that half: breaking a process into stages that hand off to each other, where each stage does exactly one job and nothing moves to the next stage without a person checking the handoff first.

citations.quote: Jake Van Clief works on that half: breaking a process into stages that hand off to each other, where each stage does exactly one job and nothing moves to the next stage without a person checking the handoff first.

slides.text: And before you walk away, test one more thing: does it still work when you're no longer in the room? Mine didn't. Three missed posts, 6am, 9am, and noon, were how I found out.
